source: Barder et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2005
summary: SPhos is a strong general-purpose ligand for coupling aryl and heteroaryl halides with aryl, heteroaryl, or vinyl boronic acids.
supporting_excerpt: The SPhos-supported catalyst gave broad and generally high-yielding Suzuki-Miyaura couplings across several electrophile and boronic-acid classes.
transferability_note: This likely transfers because the reported scope covers diverse aryl and heteroaryl partners. However, highly coordinating substrates or acutely unstable boronic acids may require a more specialized catalyst.
notes: Use SPhos as a high-priority baseline, not as a universal optimum.

source: Barder and Buchwald, Organic Letters, 2004
summary: SPhos is particularly effective for aryl or heteroaryl chlorides coupled with potassium aryl or heteroaryl trifluoroborates.
supporting_excerpt: Good to excellent coupling outcomes were reported for chloride electrophiles and potassium organotrifluoroborates using SPhos, including hindered biaryls.
transferability_note: This transfers directly to chloride plus RBF3K combinations. However, hydrolysis behavior of the individual trifluoroborate can still make base and solvent selection decisive.
notes: Prioritize SPhos in initial chloride plus organotrifluoroborate experiments.

source: Wolfe et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 1999
summary: Bulky electron-rich biphenyl phosphines can activate aryl chlorides at low temperature and low palladium loading.
supporting_excerpt: A palladium acetate and o-di-tert-butylphosphinobiphenyl system coupled aryl bromides and chlorides at room temperature.
transferability_note: This transfers because oxidative addition is commonly difficult for aryl chlorides. However, the exact ligand may not be optimal for strongly coordinating heterocycles or slow-release nucleophiles.
notes: Favor bulky electron-rich monophosphines when chloride conversion is limiting.

source: Billingsley and Buchwald, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2007
summary: Specialized monophosphine catalysts are preferred for heteroaryl-halide and heteroaryl-boron combinations, particularly with chlorides or steric hindrance.
supporting_excerpt: The optimized catalyst displayed high activity for heteroaryl boronic acids and esters, heteroaryl chlorides, and hindered aryl or heteroaryl halides.
transferability_note: This transfers to heterobiaryl formation because both partners can perturb palladium speciation. However, nitrogen position and heterocycle identity can change the preferred ligand.
notes: Escalate to a heteroaryl-optimized ligand when generic phosphines stall.

source: Kinzel et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2010
summary: A rapidly activating palladium precatalyst can improve coupling of unstable boronic acids by minimizing their exposure to degrading conditions.
supporting_excerpt: A biarylphosphine precatalyst enabled short, mild couplings of polyfluorophenyl and five-membered 2-heteroaryl boronic acids that otherwise deboronate rapidly.
transferability_note: This transfers because rapid catalyst activation reduces induction time and nucleophile loss. It may not help if hydrolysis of a protected boron reagent is the rate-limiting step.
notes: Test a rapidly activating precatalyst before increasing temperature.

source: Kinzel et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2010
summary: XPhos-type active catalyst systems are strong candidates for polyfluoroaryl and five-membered 2-heteroaryl boronic acids.
supporting_excerpt: Polyfluorophenyl, 2-furyl, 2-thienyl, and 2-pyrrolyl boronic acids were coupled with chlorides, bromides, and triflates at room temperature or 40 degrees Celsius.
transferability_note: This transfers well to similarly unstable heteroaryl and polyfluoroaryl nucleophiles. It should not be generalized to every ligand-controlled chemoselective substrate.
notes: Pair unstable nucleophiles with fast catalysts and mild temperatures.

source: Billingsley and Buchwald, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2007
summary: Coordinating heteroarenes often require ligands that preserve a reactive low-coordinate palladium species.
supporting_excerpt: Catalyst efficacy depended on the heterocyclic motif, and optimized monophosphines supported difficult heteroaryl couplings.
transferability_note: This transfers because nitrogen and sulfur heterocycles can alter palladium ligation. However, the effect depends strongly on heteroatom position and substitution.
notes: Do not treat all heteroaryl substrates as one reactivity class.

source: Hoshi et al., The Journal of Organic Chemistry, 2013
summary: Electron-rich, sterically hindered, or coordinating aryl chlorides can benefit from a long-lived bulky electron-rich phosphine catalyst.
supporting_excerpt: CyR-Phos supported coupling of aryl and heteroaryl chlorides deactivated by steric hindrance, electron richness, and coordinating functional groups.
transferability_note: This transfers to electrophiles that undergo slow oxidative addition or shorten catalyst lifetime. The exact ruthenocenyl ligand may not be available in every screening space.
notes: Use the ligand-property trend even when the exact ligand is unavailable.

source: Hoshi et al., The Journal of Organic Chemistry, 2013
summary: Extreme ortho congestion can redirect palladium chemistry away from Suzuki coupling rather than merely lowering conversion.
supporting_excerpt: An aryl bromide bearing two ortho tert-butyl groups underwent competing C(sp3)-H arylation instead of the desired Suzuki-Miyaura reaction.
transferability_note: This transfers as a warning for severely congested electrophiles because alternative palladium pathways may become competitive. The exact side reaction requires accessible nearby C-H bonds.
notes: Verify side products rather than interpreting severe congestion only as low activity.

source: Neufeldt et al., The Journal of Organic Chemistry, 2019
summary: SIPr can favor Suzuki-Miyaura coupling at aryl chloride over aryl triflate in chloroaryl triflates.
supporting_excerpt: SIPr gave preferential coupling at the chloride site across most tested chloroaryl triflates.
transferability_note: This transfers to site-selective chloroaryl-triflate coupling because ligand identity directly altered oxidative-addition selectivity. It is limited to related electrophile patterns.
notes: Use SIPr as a targeted chemoselectivity hypothesis.

source: Neufeldt et al., The Journal of Organic Chemistry, 2019
summary: SIMes can favor Suzuki-Miyaura coupling at aryl triflate over aryl chloride in chloroaryl triflates.
supporting_excerpt: SIMes provided preferential coupling at the triflate site, opposite to the selectivity obtained with SIPr.
transferability_note: This transfers because it demonstrates orthogonal ligand-controlled site selection. It should not be extrapolated to unrelated leaving-group combinations without verification.
notes: Include distinct NHC steric classes when site selectivity matters.

source: So et al., ACS Catalysis, 2021
summary: A tailored phosphine can reverse the usual electrophile preference and deliver C-Cl coupling in the presence of C-OTf.
supporting_excerpt: A Pd/L33 catalyst produced a general C-Cl greater than C-OTf reactivity order for polyhalogenated aryl triflates.
transferability_note: This transfers to chemoselective multi-electrophile substrates because ligand shape can dominate intrinsic leaving-group trends. The exact effect may not transfer to other ligand families.
notes: Do not encode C-OTf as universally more reactive than C-Cl.

source: So et al., ACS Catalysis, 2021
summary: Three-dimensional steric architecture within a phosphine can be decisive for Suzuki-Miyaura chemoselectivity.
supporting_excerpt: The methine hydrogen and steric hindrance of the alkyl lower ring in L33 were identified as key contributors to C-Cl over C-OTf selectivity.
transferability_note: This transfers as a ligand-design prior because steric shape, not only donor strength, can determine site selection. It does not define a universal steric optimum.
notes: Distinguish ligand shape from simple bulk or electron-richness labels.

source: Fujii et al., The Journal of Organic Chemistry, 2019
summary: Phosphine choice can switch the coupling position in pyrazoles containing both bromide and triflate sites.
supporting_excerpt: Different phosphine ligands reversed the preferred arylation position of 4-bromopyrazol-5-yl triflates.
transferability_note: This transfers to multifunctional heteroaryl electrophiles whose site selectivity is not captured by a simple leaving-group hierarchy. The evidence is motif-specific to pyrazoles.
notes: Use ligand-diverse screening for competing heteroaryl C-X and C-OTf sites.

source: Barder et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2005
summary: Electron-rich sterically demanding biaryl monophosphines should outrank triphenylphosphine-like ligands for difficult aryl chloride couplings.
supporting_excerpt: Ligand-structure studies linked SPhos-type ligands with broad activity toward aryl and heteroaryl halides, including less reactive electrophiles.
transferability_note: This transfers to oxidative-addition-limited electrophiles. However, the bulkiest ligand is not necessarily optimal when transmetalation or reductive elimination is limiting.
notes: Rank ligands by balanced steric and electronic properties.

source: Basu et al., Green Chemistry, 2010
summary: Ligand-free palladium conditions can be viable for aryl iodides and bromides when sodium aryl trihydroxyboronates are used in water.
supporting_excerpt: Sodium aryl trihydroxyboronates underwent ligand-free on-water coupling at ambient temperature with aryl iodides and bromides.
transferability_note: This transfers to simple reactive electrophiles and water-compatible boronates. It is less applicable to aryl chlorides, hindered substrates, or strongly coordinating heterocycles.
notes: A ligand-free branch can be reasonable when both partners are intrinsically reactive.

source: Wolfe et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 1999
summary: Aryl chloride coupling can proceed at room temperature when oxidative addition is supported by a highly electron-rich bulky monophosphine.
supporting_excerpt: The catalyst coupled aryl chlorides at room temperature, showing that high thermal forcing is not intrinsically required.
transferability_note: This transfers to thermally sensitive substrates because ligand choice can substitute for higher temperature. It may not overcome slow release from protected boron reagents.
notes: Test a more active ligand before heating a failed aryl chloride reaction.

source: Barder and Buchwald, Organic Letters, 2004
summary: SPhos is useful for coupling 3-pyridyl trifluoroborate nucleophiles with aryl and heteroaryl chlorides.
supporting_excerpt: A 3-pyridyl boron nucleophile coupled with both aryl and heteroaryl chloride electrophiles in good to very good yields.
transferability_note: This transfers directly to 3-pyridyl RBF3K combinations. It should not be assumed to solve the much faster protodeboronation of 2-pyridyl boron reagents.
notes: Differentiate 2-pyridyl and 3-pyridyl nucleophiles.

source: Kinzel et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2010
summary: Catalyst activation rate should be matched to nucleophile lifetime; unstable boronic acids favor precatalysts that generate active Pd(0) rapidly.
supporting_excerpt: The precatalyst generated the active catalyst under conditions where boronic-acid decomposition remained slow, allowing rapid productive turnover.
transferability_note: This transfers to transient nucleophiles because delayed catalyst activation wastes coupling partner. It is less relevant to stable, slowly hydrolyzing protected boronates.
notes: Treat induction time as a chemical variable when degradation is rapid.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: For sp3 boron nucleophiles, ligand systems that accelerate reductive elimination can help outcompete beta-hydride elimination.
supporting_excerpt: Slow transmetalation, protodeboronation, and beta-hydride elimination are major problems in sp3 Suzuki-Miyaura coupling, while suitable catalysts can attenuate them.
transferability_note: This transfers to primary and secondary alkyl nucleophiles because beta-hydride pathways are general. The optimal ligand still depends on alkyl structure and electrophile class.
notes: Do not directly reuse an aryl-aryl ligand optimum for alkyl coupling.

source: Carrow and Hartwig, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2011
summary: Under weak-base aqueous conditions, transmetalation is favored between an arylpalladium hydroxide and a neutral boronic acid.
supporting_excerpt: Kinetic and speciation studies identified the palladium-hydroxo plus boronic-acid route as dominant under common weak-base aqueous conditions.
transferability_note: This transfers because weak inorganic bases and aqueous cosolvents are widely used in Suzuki coupling. It should not be extrapolated to anhydrous silanolate-promoted systems.
notes: Favor conditions that form Pd-OH without accumulating excessive boronate.

source: Cox et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2016
summary: Strongly basic aqueous conditions can sharply accelerate protodeboronation for specific heteroaryl boronic acids.
supporting_excerpt: Protodeboronation rates varied by more than six orders of magnitude across heteroaryl, vinyl, and cyclopropyl boronic acids and were strongly pH-dependent.
transferability_note: This transfers whenever water and base are present. However, the hazardous pH window is substrate-specific, so one universal base ranking is inappropriate.
notes: Treat base as a stability control as well as a transmetalation activator.

source: Cox et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2016
summary: 2-Pyridyl and 5-thiazolyl boronic acids are acutely vulnerable in aqueous media and should not be exposed to reaction conditions for long periods.
supporting_excerpt: At 70 degrees Celsius and pH 7, 2-pyridyl and 5-thiazolyl boronic acids showed half-lives on the order of tens of seconds.
transferability_note: This transfers directly to these heteroaryl motifs because their decomposition is intrinsically fast. Exact rates change with temperature, solvent composition, and substitution.
notes: Use masked nucleophiles, mild temperature, and rapid turnover.

source: Cox et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2016
summary: 3-Pyridyl and 4-pyridyl boronic acids are substantially more tolerant of basic aqueous conditions than 2-pyridyl analogues.
supporting_excerpt: 3- and 4-pyridyl boronic acids underwent very slow protodeboronation even at pH 12 and 70 degrees Celsius, unlike the 2-pyridyl isomer.
transferability_note: This transfers because heteroatom position controls the decomposition pathway. Substitution can still alter stability, so positional class remains an advisory prior.
notes: Do not penalize all pyridyl boronic acids equally.

source: Chen et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2017
summary: Acutely base-sensitive polyfluoroaryl and heteroaryl boronic acids can benefit from cationic Suzuki-Miyaura conditions that reduce reliance on conventional base.
supporting_excerpt: The cationic coupling strategy was developed because standard base promotes rapid protodeboronation of polyfluoroaryl and heteroaryl boronic acids.
transferability_note: This transfers to nucleophiles that decompose faster than they transmetalate under standard basic conditions. Specialized catalyst and counterion requirements limit universal application.
notes: Include a low-base or cationic branch when decomposition dominates.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: Base and heat accelerate MIDA-boronate hydrolysis, so both variables control release of the active boronic acid.
supporting_excerpt: MIDA boronates hydrolyze slowly in protic media, while heating or adding base substantially accelerates deprotection.
transferability_note: This transfers because MIDA reagents generally act as masked boronic acids. The optimum release rate depends on catalyst turnover and stability of the liberated acid.
notes: Screen base strength and temperature together for MIDA nucleophiles.

source: Knapp et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2009
summary: Overly rapid MIDA hydrolysis can erase its slow-release advantage and recreate decomposition of the free boronic acid.
supporting_excerpt: The benefit of MIDA boronates arose from gradual release of unstable boronic acids, which maintained a low concentration during coupling.
transferability_note: This transfers to unstable heteroaryl, vinyl, and cyclopropyl nucleophiles. It is less important for robust boronic acids for which rapid release may be beneficial.
notes: Diagnose whether MIDA release is too slow or too fast.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2012
summary: Organotrifluoroborate hydrolysis must be kinetically matched to catalytic turnover; release that is too fast or too slow can reduce yield.
supporting_excerpt: RBF3K reagents displayed substrate-dependent hydrolysis profiles, and slow release was useful only when reagent release and catalytic consumption were properly geared.
transferability_note: This transfers broadly to organotrifluoroborates because the protected reagent is normally not the most reactive transmetalating species. Physical phase behavior can change the rate.
notes: Low conversion may reflect an activation-rate mismatch rather than poor catalyst activity.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2012
summary: Cs2CO3 in THF-water gives strongly substrate-dependent organotrifluoroborate hydrolysis, so one recipe is not general across R groups.
supporting_excerpt: Under THF, water, Cs2CO3, and 55 degrees Celsius, different RBF3K reagents showed fast, slow, very slow, or complex solvolytic behavior.
transferability_note: This transfers directly to Cs2CO3-based trifluoroborate screens. However, the measured categories are specific to the reported solvent and temperature regime.
notes: Stratify RBF3K substrates by hydrolysis behavior.

source: Denmark et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2022
summary: Potassium trimethylsilanolate can promote anhydrous Suzuki-Miyaura coupling through a boronate pathway distinct from common aqueous systems.
supporting_excerpt: Isolated-intermediate and kinetic studies showed that TMSOK-promoted anhydrous coupling proceeds through reaction of a boronate with an arylpalladium halide.
transferability_note: This transfers to water-sensitive substrates and deliberately anhydrous conditions. It should not be interpreted using the weak-base aqueous palladium-hydroxide mechanism.
notes: Treat TMSOK as a distinct condition family.

source: Carrow and Hartwig, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2011
summary: Changing the base can change the active palladium and boron species, not merely the bulk pH.
supporting_excerpt: The dominant transmetalation route depended on the populations and reaction rates of palladium-hydroxo, palladium-halide, boronic-acid, and boronate species.
transferability_note: This transfers broadly because base identity controls speciation and kinetics. The evidence is strongest for weak-base aqueous mixtures.
notes: Represent base as a mechanistic category rather than only a basicity value.

source: Carrow and Hartwig, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2011
summary: Weak bases in aqueous solvent can support productive Pd-OH formation without requiring a high concentration of trihydroxyboronate.
supporting_excerpt: Neutral boronic acid and palladium-hydroxo species accounted for productive transmetalation under typical weak-base catalytic conditions.
transferability_note: This transfers to base-sensitive substrates because weak-base conditions may preserve the nucleophile while maintaining catalytic activation. It may fail if oxidative addition is too slow.
notes: Include weak inorganic bases rather than screening only hydroxide.

source: Cox et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2017
summary: Very high pH can open fast base-catalyzed protodeboronation pathways for arylboronic acids that are stable under milder conditions.
supporting_excerpt: Kinetic studies of 30 arylboronic acids at pH above 13 identified base-catalyzed decomposition involving transient aryl-anion character.
transferability_note: This transfers as a warning against excessive hydroxide or strongly basic aqueous conditions. It does not directly predict behavior with mild carbonate or phosphate bases.
notes: Increasing base strength can reduce yield even if transmetalation is accelerated.

source: Hayes et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2021
summary: Boronic-ester stability in basic aqueous media depends strongly on pH, ester diol, and the attached aryl or heteroaryl group.
supporting_excerpt: Eight polyol ester classes and ten aryl or heteroaryl groups displayed nuanced hydrolysis and protodeboronation through direct and prehydrolytic pathways.
transferability_note: This transfers to boronic esters generally because both ester structure and organic group matter. A universal BPin-versus-boronic-acid ranking is not reliable.
notes: Use motif-specific evidence when selecting the boron form.

source: Hayes et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2021
summary: Esterifying a boronic acid does not necessarily make its carbon-boron bond more stable under basic aqueous coupling conditions.
supporting_excerpt: Boronic-ester formation was found not to confer greater phenomenological stability than the corresponding boronic acid in every case.
transferability_note: This transfers as a correction to a common reagent-selection assumption. Stability remains dependent on ester class, pH, and the attached organic fragment.
notes: Do not automatically rank every boronic ester above its free acid.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2012
summary: Base-induced phase splitting can alter the effective pH and hydrolysis rate of organotrifluoroborates.
supporting_excerpt: Cs2CO3 partially split THF-water into phases, changed the local acidity, and made hydrolysis dependent on physical mixing.
transferability_note: This transfers to heterogeneous screening wells where salt loading changes phase behavior. The exact effect depends on solvent ratio, geometry, and agitation.
notes: Record phase state and mixing quality for RBF3K experiments.

source: Chen et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2017
summary: When conventional base destroys the nucleophile, a base-minimized catalytic manifold may be preferable to further base optimization.
supporting_excerpt: The cationic method bypassed the conflict between the usual catalytic need for base and rapid base-promoted protodeboronation.
transferability_note: This transfers when analytical data show that decomposition increases with base strength. It requires access to a specialized cationic catalyst regime.
notes: Leave the standard carbonate or phosphate family when decomposition dominates.

source: Basu et al., Green Chemistry, 2010
summary: Preformed sodium aryl trihydroxyboronates can support nominally base-free Suzuki-Miyaura coupling.
supporting_excerpt: Stable tetrahedral aryl trihydroxyboronate salts underwent clean ligand-free and externally base-free coupling in water.
transferability_note: This transfers because the nucleophile is already a tetrahedral boronate. It should not be generalized to neutral boronic acids or esters without considering catalyst activation.
notes: Consider preactivated boronates when external base threatens sensitive functionality.

source: Carrillo et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2016
summary: KOH in biphasic THF-water can provide controlled MIDA hydrolysis suitable for slow-release Suzuki-Miyaura processes.
supporting_excerpt: Optimized KOH conditions in biphasic THF-water slowly released thienyl boronic acids from MIDA monomers and supported effective coupling polymerization.
transferability_note: This transfers to thienyl and related MIDA boronates because controlled hydrolysis is the same activation step. Polymerization kinetics limit direct quantitative extrapolation.
notes: Treat KOH loading and phase ratio as interacting variables.

source: Knapp et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2009
summary: Maintaining a low concentration of an unstable boronic acid can suppress protodeboronation and nonproductive homocoupling.
supporting_excerpt: Slow release from MIDA boronates converted unstable heterocyclic, vinyl, and cyclopropyl boronic acids into effective coupling partners.
transferability_note: This transfers because many boronic-acid side reactions depend on concentration and exposure time. It can be counterproductive if release becomes slower than catalytic consumption.
notes: Low steady-state free-boronic-acid concentration is a useful design objective.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: Water is usually required as a cosolvent for organotrifluoroborates because hydrolysis precedes productive transmetalation.
supporting_excerpt: Most successful organotrifluoroborate protocols use water-containing media to reveal the corresponding boronic acid before coupling.
transferability_note: This transfers broadly to RBF3K nucleophiles because hydrolysis is normally required. The optimum water fraction remains dependent on the substrate and base.
notes: Treat water content as an activation variable for trifluoroborates.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: Trace water in an alcoholic solvent can improve organotrifluoroborate coupling by assisting hydrolysis.
supporting_excerpt: Bench-grade alcohol sometimes gave better yields than rigorously dry alcohol, consistent with residual water assisting RBF3K activation.
transferability_note: This transfers as a practical solvent-quality prior for trifluoroborates. The effect may reverse for water-sensitive electrophiles or catalyst systems.
notes: Record solvent dryness when results are difficult to reproduce.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: Anhydrous solvent can keep an organotrifluoroborate latent while a more reactive organoboron group couples first.
supporting_excerpt: Organotrifluoroborates remained inert in anhydrous media during orthogonal sequences in which an organoborane reacted first.
transferability_note: This transfers to molecules containing more than one boron functionality because solvent can gate activation. Orthogonality must still be validated for the exact reagents.
notes: Use dry conditions deliberately when the trifluoroborate should be preserved.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: Switching from anhydrous to aqueous or alcoholic medium can activate an organotrifluoroborate in a later Suzuki-Miyaura step.
supporting_excerpt: Sequential coupling was achieved by changing to a hydrolytic medium that exposed the boronic acid from RBF3K.
transferability_note: This transfers to staged or iterative coupling plans. The activation rate can still vary widely with the organic group and base.
notes: Solvent switching can be a chemoselective control strategy.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: THF-water can preserve alkenyltrifluoroborate geometry better than an alcoholic medium in some Suzuki-Miyaura systems.
supporting_excerpt: Alkenyltrifluoroborate transmetalation proceeded with retention in THF-water, whereas an alcohol-based system showed attenuated stereoselectivity.
transferability_note: This transfers to stereodefined alkenyl nucleophiles because solvent can influence stereochemical fidelity. Catalyst identity also differed, limiting attribution to solvent alone.
notes: Verify E/Z ratios after changing solvent families.

source: Carrow and Hartwig, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2011
summary: Aqueous-organic biphasic media can support productive speciation by retaining neutral boronic acid while enabling palladium-hydroxide formation.
supporting_excerpt: Under weak-base aqueous mixtures, the productive species were consistent with neutral boronic acid and arylpalladium hydroxide.
transferability_note: This transfers to common THF-water and dioxane-water protocols. It is less applicable to fully homogeneous polar media or anhydrous systems.
notes: Biphasic behavior is not necessarily detrimental to coupling.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2012
summary: Vessel geometry and stirring can alter organotrifluoroborate hydrolysis in phase-separated THF-water mixtures.
supporting_excerpt: Hydrolysis profiles depended on vessel shape, material, size, and stirring because phase splitting controlled local acidity and mass transfer.
transferability_note: This transfers directly to high-throughput or scale-changing experiments using RBF3K reagents. The sensitivity is greatest in partially phase-separated systems.
notes: Do not interpret mixing-dependent differences solely as molecular effects.

source: Lipshutz et al., ACS Catalysis, 2017
summary: Micellar water can enable mild copper-free Suzuki-Miyaura coupling of selected 2-pyridyl MIDA boronates.
supporting_excerpt: Selected halogen-substituted 2-pyridyl MIDA boronates coupled in water under micellar conditions without copper.
transferability_note: This transfers to similarly substituted 2-pyridyl MIDA reagents because micelles and ring substitution attenuate problematic coordination. Unsubstituted analogues may behave differently.
notes: Micellar water is a specialized option for difficult 2-pyridyl substrates.

source: Isley et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2013
summary: MIDA-boronate Suzuki-Miyaura coupling can be performed with water as the only reaction medium, often near room temperature.
supporting_excerpt: The reported technology used water throughout the reaction and isolation for a range of MIDA-boronate couplings, mainly at room temperature.
transferability_note: This transfers as evidence that organic solvent is not intrinsically required for MIDA activation. Surfactant, catalyst, and substrate-solubility requirements remain important.
notes: Include aqueous media when substrate and catalyst formulation permit.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: A modest amount of water can improve pinacol-boronate coupling by promoting hydrolysis or formation of a palladium-oxo intermediate.
supporting_excerpt: Pinacol boronic esters often coupled more reliably after adding a small amount of water, although direct ester transmetalation can occur in some systems.
transferability_note: This transfers to BPin nucleophiles because water can reveal a more reactive species or support Pd-OH formation. Excess water may create phase or hydrolysis problems.
notes: Test controlled water fractions rather than only dry versus wet conditions.

source: Thomas et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2018
summary: Nominally anhydrous boronic-ester coupling can still depend on adventitious water, so water content should be explicitly controlled.
supporting_excerpt: Structural and kinetic investigations identified multiple activation modes for boronic esters and highlighted the importance of hydrolysis state.
transferability_note: This transfers because trace water can alter boron speciation even when no water is intentionally added. The magnitude depends on ester class and base.
notes: Standardize or measure water content in mechanistic comparisons.

source: Denmark et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2022
summary: Anhydrous TMSOK-promoted coupling is a useful condition family for substrates that should not be exposed to aqueous media.
supporting_excerpt: The TMSOK system operated without water and used a boronate-pathway transmetalation mechanism.
transferability_note: This transfers to water-sensitive functional groups and selected boronic esters. It may not suit substrates incompatible with strongly nucleophilic silanolate.
notes: Include a dry branch when aqueous activation damages the substrate.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2012
summary: Solvent polarity and phase partitioning can determine how quickly an organotrifluoroborate reaches the aqueous hydrolysis region.
supporting_excerpt: RBF3K hydrolysis depended on both intrinsic structure and partitioning between organic-rich and aqueous-rich phases.
transferability_note: This transfers because hydrophilic and hydrophobic trifluoroborates encounter different local environments. Exact partitioning depends on concentration and solvent ratio.
notes: Consider nucleophile polarity when selecting solvent composition.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: Organotrifluoroborate salts are often poorly soluble in apolar solvents, creating mass-transfer limitations even with an active catalyst.
supporting_excerpt: Low solubility in many apolar solvents is a major practical limitation of potassium organotrifluoroborates.
transferability_note: This transfers directly to heterogeneous screening conditions. Water, alcohol, or phase-transfer changes can improve access but also alter hydrolysis kinetics.
notes: Separate solubility failure from intrinsic nucleophile reactivity.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: Neutral boronic acids often prefer an organic-rich phase over neutral water, so solvent ratio controls both availability and boronate formation.
supporting_excerpt: Boronic acids generally dissolve more readily in organic solvent than neutral water, while their boronate forms favor more aqueous environments.
transferability_note: This transfers to biphasic Suzuki systems because speciation and partitioning are linked. Highly polar heteroaryl boronic acids may deviate from the trend.
notes: Balance organic-phase substrate access with aqueous-phase base activation.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: Free boronic acids are usually highly reactive nucleophiles but are more exposed to oxidation, homocoupling, and protodeboronation than masked forms.
supporting_excerpt: Boronic acids were the most reactive species in competition studies, while protected reagents often improved outcome by suppressing side reactions.
transferability_note: This transfers as a general reactivity-versus-stability tradeoff. The preferred form depends on the organic group and catalyst turnover rate.
notes: Prefer free acids for robust motifs and masked forms for short-lived motifs.

source: Thomas et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2018
summary: Pinacol boronic esters offer handling stability but may require hydrolysis or specific base activation before efficient transmetalation.
supporting_excerpt: Kinetic and structural studies showed that boronic esters can react through several pathways and that their active form is condition-dependent.
transferability_note: This transfers to BPin-containing reaction spaces because ester identity cannot be separated from base and water. It does not establish one universal hydrolysis requirement.
notes: Screen BPin under both hydrolytic and deliberately anhydrous activation regimes.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: Neopentyl-glycol boronic esters can be more reactive than pinacol esters, although both may remain less reactive than the corresponding boronic acid.
supporting_excerpt: Competition experiments consumed more neopentyl-glycol ester than pinacol ester, while the free boronic acid was the most reactive reagent.
transferability_note: This transfers as an ester-class ranking prior. The order may change with base, ligand, substrate electronics, and the need for hydrolysis.
notes: Do not collapse all boronic esters into one category.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: Potassium organotrifluoroborates should be treated as protected boronic acids whose productive coupling normally follows hydrolysis.
supporting_excerpt: The trifluoroborate was not the fastest transmetalating species, and the boronic acid produced by hydrolysis was more reactive.
transferability_note: This transfers broadly to RBF3K reagents. Mixed fluoro-hydroxy intermediates may occur, but hydrolysis remains a central activation event.
notes: Evaluate RBF3K conditions by release kinetics, not only reagent stability.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: Slow release from organotrifluoroborates can improve yield by suppressing oxidative homocoupling, oxidation, and protodeboronation.
supporting_excerpt: Low steady-state boronic-acid concentration and released fluoride reduced several side-product pathways relative to direct use of the free acid.
transferability_note: This transfers to unstable or oxidation-prone nucleophiles. If hydrolysis is excessively slow, conversion may instead be limited by reagent activation.
notes: Use side-product profiles to distinguish slow release from unproductive latency.

source: Knapp et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2009
summary: MIDA boronates are strong choices for unstable 2-heterocyclic, vinyl, and cyclopropyl boronic-acid equivalents.
supporting_excerpt: Air-stable MIDA boronates converted three classes of inherently unstable boronic acids into shelf-stable and effective coupling partners.
transferability_note: This transfers directly when the current nucleophile belongs to these instability-prone classes. The hydrolysis conditions may still be incompatible with some electrophiles.
notes: Rank MIDA forms highly when free-acid stability is problematic.

source: Knapp et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2009
summary: For 2-furyl nucleophiles, controlled slow release can outperform rapid release or direct use of freshly prepared boronic acid.
supporting_excerpt: Slow release from 2-furyl MIDA boronate improved coupling, and slow syringe addition of the free acid reproduced the benefit.
transferability_note: This transfers strongly to 2-furyl and similarly short-lived heteroaryl boronic acids. It may not help robust acids whose concentration is not a liability.
notes: Controlled feed and masked release are related optimization hypotheses.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: 2-Pyridyl MIDA boronates often require an integrated strategy combining fast catalysis, controlled release, and sometimes boron-activating additives.
supporting_excerpt: Successful 2-pyridyl MIDA coupling combined a rapidly activating biarylphosphine precatalyst, masking, slow release, and in some cases copper or silver assistance.
transferability_note: This transfers because no single variable resolves all failure modes of the 2-pyridyl motif. Additive requirements depend on substitution and catalyst family.
notes: Use multivariable experiments rather than ligand-only scans.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: N-coordinated boronates can stabilize 2-pyridyl groups against protodeboronation more effectively than the free boronic acid.
supporting_excerpt: Diethanolamine and related N-coordinated boronates allowed 2-pyridyl fragments to be incorporated despite the instability of 2-pyridylboronic acid.
transferability_note: This transfers to 2-pyridyl and related internally coordinating heteroaryl groups. Release and transmetalation conditions remain reagent-specific.
notes: Masked tetracoordinate forms should outrank free 2-pyridylboronic acid.

source: Cox et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2016
summary: Unsubstituted 2-pyridylboronic acid is a high-risk nucleophile because intramolecularly assisted protodeboronation is exceptionally fast.
supporting_excerpt: 2-Pyridylboronic acid decomposed within seconds under representative aqueous conditions through a zwitterionic fragmentation pathway.
transferability_note: This transfers directly to the 2-pyridyl motif. Substitution can attenuate or accelerate the process, so the exact rate should not be assumed.
notes: Flag free 2-pyridylboronic acids before batch execution.

source: Cox et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2016
summary: 5-Thiazolylboronic acid is a high-risk heteroaryl nucleophile that can protodeboronate on the same timescale as 2-pyridylboronic acid.
supporting_excerpt: 5-Thiazolylboronic acid showed rapid fragmentation at near-neutral pH and elevated temperature.
transferability_note: This transfers to 5-thiazolyl nucleophiles because heteroatom arrangement strongly destabilizes the C-B bond. Other thiazole positions require separate assessment.
notes: Use masked forms, mild temperature, and fast turnover.

source: Cox et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2016
summary: Vinyl and cyclopropyl boronic acids can be more resistant to aqueous protodeboronation than commonly assumed.
supporting_excerpt: The measured vinyl and cyclopropyl boronic acids underwent very slow protodeboronation compared with the most unstable heteroaryl examples.
transferability_note: This transfers as a correction against over-penalizing these classes for protodeboronation alone. Polymerization, isomerization, and other side reactions remain possible.
notes: Separate C-B stability from other nucleophile-specific risks.

source: Kinzel et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2010
summary: Polyfluorophenyl boronic acids require rapid mild coupling because their electron-deficient rings can undergo fast base-promoted protodeboronation.
supporting_excerpt: A fast precatalyst coupled polyfluorophenyl boronic acids at room temperature or 40 degrees Celsius before substantial decomposition occurred.
transferability_note: This transfers to highly fluorinated aryl boronic acids. Less fluorinated analogues may be more stable and require less specialized conditions.
notes: Avoid prolonged heating as the first response to low conversion.

source: Molander and Bernardi, The Journal of Organic Chemistry, 2002
summary: Alkenyltrifluoroborates are practical stereodefined nucleophiles for Suzuki-Miyaura coupling.
supporting_excerpt: Potassium alkenyltrifluoroborates coupled in moderate to excellent yields and retained useful alkene stereochemical information under appropriate conditions.
transferability_note: This transfers to alkenyl RBF3K building blocks. Stereochemical fidelity still depends on solvent and catalyst conditions.
notes: Preserve and verify E/Z labels throughout optimization.

source: Molander et al., The Journal of Organic Chemistry, 2002
summary: Potassium alkynyltrifluoroborates can serve as air-stable nucleophiles for aryl alkynylation by Suzuki-Miyaura coupling.
supporting_excerpt: Aryl halides and triflates coupled with potassium alkynyltrifluoroborates in moderate to excellent yields.
transferability_note: This transfers directly to alkynyl RBF3K nucleophiles and aryl electrophiles. Some alkynyltrifluoroborates hydrolyze slowly and may need stronger activation.
notes: Do not exclude alkynyl boron nucleophiles solely because Sonogashira coupling is more common.

source: Dreher et al., The Journal of Organic Chemistry, 2009
summary: Primary alkyltrifluoroborates can be coupled with aryl chlorides when an alkyl-specific catalyst system is used.
supporting_excerpt: A tailored palladium protocol established Suzuki-Miyaura coupling of primary alkyltrifluoroborates with aryl chlorides.
transferability_note: This transfers directly to primary alkyl RBF3K plus aryl chloride combinations. Secondary and tertiary alkyl nucleophiles present additional stereochemical and beta-hydride challenges.
notes: Use a dedicated sp3-coupling condition branch.

source: Molander and Shin, Organic Letters, 2012
summary: Boc-protected secondary aminomethyltrifluoroborates are viable nucleophiles for aryl and heteroaryl chlorides.
supporting_excerpt: A broad set of aryl and hetaryl chlorides furnished secondary aminomethyl products in good to excellent yields.
transferability_note: This transfers to protected aminomethyl RBF3K reagents because both nucleophile and electrophile classes match. Other amine protecting groups may change compatibility.
notes: Protected aminomethyl motifs are not intrinsically incompatible with chlorides.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: Organotrifluoroborates can reduce protodeboronation risk in sp3 coupling, but they do not remove beta-hydride-elimination risk.
supporting_excerpt: RBF3K stability helped enable sp3 couplings, while suitable catalysts were still required to outcompete beta-hydride elimination.
transferability_note: This transfers to alkyl nucleophiles bearing beta hydrogens. The risk is lower for methyl or structurally constrained alkyl groups.
notes: Check for alkene and isomerized side products.

source: Basu et al., Green Chemistry, 2010
summary: Sodium aryl trihydroxyboronates are air-stable water-compatible nucleophiles that can couple without added ligand or external base.
supporting_excerpt: Stable sodium aryl trihydroxyboronate salts promoted ligand-free on-water coupling at ambient temperature for reactive aryl halides.
transferability_note: This transfers to simple aryl trihydroxyboronates. Heteroaryl, alkyl, or chloride combinations may require different catalysts or higher temperature.
notes: Treat trihydroxyboronates as a distinct nucleophile family.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: MIDA boronates are incompatible with hard nucleophiles and strong alkoxide or fluoride reagents that can disrupt the tetracoordinate boron complex.
supporting_excerpt: MIDA boronates were reported to be incompatible with LiAlH4, DIBAL, TBAF, and metal alkoxides, although they tolerate many milder transformations.
transferability_note: This transfers as a compatibility warning when strong nucleophilic bases or additives are considered. Controlled hydroxide hydrolysis is a different regime.
notes: Avoid harsh fluoride or alkoxide activation without direct precedent.

source: Hayes et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2021
summary: Heteroaryl and polyfluoroaryl boronic esters may protodeboronate directly from the ester or after hydrolysis to the acid.
supporting_excerpt: Direct and prehydrolytic decomposition pathways were both relevant, depending on ester structure and the attached aryl group.
transferability_note: This transfers to stability diagnosis because suppressing hydrolysis will not always suppress decomposition. The dominant pathway depends on motif and conditions.
notes: A stable free acid concentration does not prove that the ester is stable.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: Boronic acids can partially dehydrate to boroxines, making the effective nucleophile stoichiometry uncertain.
supporting_excerpt: Under nominally anhydrous conditions, boronic acids establish an equilibrium with trimeric boroxines and release water.
transferability_note: This transfers to reagent weighing because stored or commercial boronic acids may contain variable boroxine content. The equilibrium depends on solvent and water activity.
notes: Verify assay or allow a modest stoichiometric margin.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: A modest excess of boronic acid is often practical because the nucleophile can be lost through dehydration or side reactions before coupling.
supporting_excerpt: Variable boroxine formation and competing boronic-acid degradation make exact productive equivalents difficult to guarantee in some systems.
transferability_note: This transfers as a general stoichiometric prior. Excess should be limited for expensive nucleophiles or when homocoupling is substantial.
notes: Treat nucleophile equivalents as an optimization variable.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2012
summary: Nitrophenyl and some alkynyl trifluoroborates can hydrolyze extremely slowly under standard basic aqueous conditions.
supporting_excerpt: Nitrophenyl and alkynyl RBF3K examples were among the very slow hydrolyzers in the THF-water-Cs2CO3 study.
transferability_note: This transfers to related substituent classes because reagent activation can become turnover-limiting. Alternative solvent or acid-promoted hydrolysis may change the ranking.
notes: Change activation conditions before assuming catalyst failure.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2012
summary: Isopropyl, beta-styryl, and anisyl trifluoroborates can release boronic acid relatively rapidly under hydrolytic conditions.
supporting_excerpt: These RBF3K examples showed efficient direct hydrolysis compared with slower classes under THF-water-Cs2CO3 conditions.
transferability_note: This transfers as a relative hydrolysis prior for closely related R groups. Rates remain sensitive to solvent ratio, temperature, and mixing.
notes: Fast hydrolysis may reduce the side-reaction protection expected from slow release.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2012
summary: p-Fluorophenyl, naphthyl, furyl, and benzyl trifluoroborates may require acid-catalyzed hydrolysis even in an overall basic Suzuki medium.
supporting_excerpt: These reagents displayed an acid-base paradox in which efficient hydrolysis depended on acidic microenvironments in a nominally basic phase-separated mixture.
transferability_note: This transfers to related RBF3K nucleophiles because local phase chemistry can dominate bulk pH. Behavior may change in homogeneous solvent systems.
notes: Bulk pH alone is insufficient to predict trifluoroborate activation.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2012
summary: Vinyltrifluoroborate can hydrolyze rapidly because its hydrophilicity drives partitioning into the aqueous phase.
supporting_excerpt: Vinyl-BF3K was an exception to simple electronic trends because it accumulated in the aqueous minor phase and hydrolyzed quickly.
transferability_note: This transfers to unusually hydrophilic organotrifluoroborates. Counterion, concentration, and solvent ratio can alter the partitioning behavior.
notes: Include physical partitioning when ranking RBF3K activation rates.

source: Basu et al., Green Chemistry, 2010
summary: Under ligand-free on-water conditions with trihydroxyboronates, aryl iodides and bromides react readily at room temperature whereas chlorides require more forcing conditions.
supporting_excerpt: The method accommodated iodides and bromides at ambient temperature, while chloride electrophiles required elevated temperature.
transferability_note: This transfers as an electrophile-reactivity prior within ligand-free aqueous systems. A strong modern ligand can substantially change chloride reactivity.
notes: Do not transfer room-temperature iodide or bromide results directly to chlorides.

source: Wolfe et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 1999
summary: Aryl chlorides should generally be paired with more electron-rich and sterically demanding ligands than aryl bromides when oxidative addition is slow.
supporting_excerpt: A bulky biphenyl phosphine catalyst activated both bromides and the less reactive chloride electrophiles at room temperature.
transferability_note: This transfers because C-Cl oxidative addition is generally more demanding. Electron-poor or highly coordinating chlorides may still need specialized catalysts.
notes: Stratify ligand screening by electrophile class.

source: Barder and Buchwald, Organic Letters, 2004
summary: Heteroaryl chlorides can be competent electrophiles when paired with SPhos and an appropriately activated boron reagent.
supporting_excerpt: SPhos supported coupling of heteroaryl chlorides with aryl and heteroaryl trifluoroborates in good to excellent yields.
transferability_note: This transfers to chloride-bearing heterocycles because the electrophile class matches. Strongly coordinating substitution patterns may still inhibit the catalyst.
notes: Do not automatically downgrade all heteroaryl chlorides to infeasible.

source: Billingsley and Buchwald, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2007
summary: Sterically hindered aryl and heteroaryl halides benefit from highly active monophosphine catalysts rather than generic low-activity systems.
supporting_excerpt: The optimized monophosphine system coupled hindered aryl and heteroaryl halides and showed high activity toward heteroaryl chlorides.
transferability_note: This transfers to ortho-substituted or fused electrophiles. Extreme congestion can still generate alternative pathways rather than simple low conversion.
notes: Include a high-activity bulky monophosphine for hindered electrophiles.

source: Hoshi et al., The Journal of Organic Chemistry, 2013
summary: Electron-rich aryl chlorides are comparatively deactivated electrophiles and often require a stronger oxidative-addition catalyst.
supporting_excerpt: CyR-Phos was developed to couple aryl chlorides deactivated by electron richness as well as steric and coordinating effects.
transferability_note: This transfers because electron-rich C-Cl bonds undergo slower oxidative addition to Pd(0). The magnitude depends on substitution and ligand donor strength.
notes: Use electrophile electron richness as a reason to escalate ligand activity.

source: Hoshi et al., The Journal of Organic Chemistry, 2013
summary: Electrophiles containing coordinating functional groups can shorten catalyst lifetime even when the carbon-halogen bond is not highly hindered.
supporting_excerpt: A long-lived CyR-Phos catalyst was effective for chloride electrophiles bearing coordinating functionality that deactivated conventional systems.
transferability_note: This transfers as a catalyst-poisoning prior for donor-rich substrates. Coordination strength and the position of the donor group are important boundaries.
notes: Distinguish catalyst poisoning from intrinsically slow oxidative addition.

source: Neufeldt et al., The Journal of Organic Chemistry, 2019
summary: Chemoselectivity in polyfunctional electrophiles is ligand-dependent and should be verified rather than inferred only from leaving-group identity.
supporting_excerpt: SIPr and SIMes delivered opposite site selectivity for the same chloroaryl-triflate electrophile class.
transferability_note: This transfers to multi-electrophile molecules because catalyst ligation changes oxidative-addition pathways. The exact selectivity map remains substrate-specific.
notes: Require site-selectivity verification for polyhalogenated substrates.

source: So et al., ACS Catalysis, 2021
summary: C-Cl versus C-OTf reactivity order is not intrinsic; a tailored ligand can make chloride the preferred coupling site.
supporting_excerpt: Pd/L33 delivered broad C-Cl-selective Suzuki-Miyaura coupling in the presence of aryl triflates.
transferability_note: This transfers directly to staged functionalization of chloroaryl triflates. Other ligand families may restore the opposite selectivity.
notes: Encode leaving-group competition as a ligand-electrophile interaction.

source: Kinzel et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2010
summary: Aryl triflates can be coupled with highly unstable boronic acids under mild and fast catalyst conditions.
supporting_excerpt: A rapidly activating precatalyst coupled chlorides, bromides, and triflates with polyfluoroaryl and 2-heteroaryl boronic acids at low temperature.
transferability_note: This transfers to triflate electrophiles paired with short-lived nucleophiles. Triflate hydrolysis remains a possible competing pathway in more strongly basic aqueous conditions.
notes: Prefer short low-temperature cycles when both partners are condition-sensitive.

source: Kinzel et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2010
summary: A single fast biarylphosphine precatalyst can cover chlorides, bromides, and triflates when nucleophile instability is the dominant challenge.
supporting_excerpt: The method showed broad electrophile-class compatibility while maintaining rapid turnover of unstable boronic acids.
transferability_note: This transfers as a batch-composition prior because several mono-electrophile classes can share one catalyst family. Multi-electrophile substrates require separate selectivity validation.
notes: Group simple electrophiles only when catalyst and temperature are compatible.

source: Burns et al., Organic Letters, 2007
summary: Benzylic halides can participate in Suzuki-Miyaura coupling, but they require catalyst systems validated for sp3 electrophiles.
supporting_excerpt: A defined palladium(II) precatalyst coupled benzylic halides with aryl and heteroaryl boronic acids.
transferability_note: This transfers to benzylic electrophiles because their oxidative addition and side reactions differ from aryl halides. Unactivated alkyl halides should not be inferred to behave similarly.
notes: Classify benzylic halides separately from aryl and vinyl electrophiles.

source: Basu et al., Green Chemistry, 2010
summary: With water-compatible trihydroxyboronates, iodide and bromide electrophiles are easier than chlorides under ligand-free conditions.
supporting_excerpt: Ambient-temperature coupling was effective for aryl iodides and bromides, while aryl chlorides required heating.
transferability_note: This transfers within low-ligand aqueous systems. Modern electron-rich ligands can narrow or reverse the practical difference.
notes: Use electrophile class to define initial temperature tiers.

source: Dreher et al., The Journal of Organic Chemistry, 2009
summary: Aryl chloride plus primary alkyltrifluoroborate is a doubly demanding pairing that benefits from an alkyl-specific ligand and hydrolytic solvent system.
supporting_excerpt: Successful coupling required a protocol developed specifically for primary alkyltrifluoroborates and aryl chlorides.
transferability_note: This transfers directly because both slow chloride activation and sp3 transmetalation must be addressed. Secondary alkyl reagents may need different stereochemical controls.
notes: The electrophile-nucleophile interaction is the central difficulty.

source: Billingsley and Buchwald, Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2007
summary: Heteroaryl-halide plus heteroaryl-boron combinations warrant specialized ligand screening because both partners can coordinate or decompose.
supporting_excerpt: The catalyst system was optimized for heteroaryl halides with heteroaryl boronic acids and esters and tolerated several difficult motifs.
transferability_note: This transfers directly to heterobiaryl targets. Nitrogen position, sulfur content, and boron form remain important limitations.
notes: Allocate more ligand diversity to heteroaryl-heteroaryl pairs.

source: Barder et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2005
summary: SPhos can support formation of sterically hindered biaryls, making it a strong initial ligand for ortho-substituted coupling partners.
supporting_excerpt: The SPhos catalyst displayed broad scope that included hindered aryl and heteroaryl coupling combinations.
transferability_note: This transfers to moderate ortho congestion because bulky monophosphines can maintain reactive low-coordinate palladium. Extreme congestion can still cause alternative chemistry.
notes: Include an alternative ligand shape for severe congestion.

source: Neufeldt et al., The Journal of Organic Chemistry, 2019
summary: Sequential functionalization of multi-electrophile substrates can exploit ligand-controlled site selectivity rather than relying only on temperature staging.
supporting_excerpt: Orthogonal NHC ligands selected either the chloride or triflate site in the same electrophile class.
transferability_note: This transfers to stepwise synthesis because changing ligand can expose a different reaction site while preserving another handle. Each substrate topology still requires validation.
notes: Treat ligand switching as a sequencing tool.

source: Kinzel et al., Journal of the American Chemical Society, 2010
summary: When an unstable boronic acid is used, choose an electrophile-ligand combination that produces reactive palladium(II) faster than the nucleophile decomposes.
supporting_excerpt: A fast precatalyst coupled unstable nucleophiles with chlorides, bromides, and triflates under mild short-time conditions.
transferability_note: This transfers because productive palladium(II) must accumulate before nucleophile loss. It may not solve cases where hydrolysis of a protected boron reagent is slower than turnover.
notes: Balance electrophile activation rate against nucleophile lifetime.

source: Lennox and Lloyd-Jones, Chemical Society Reviews, 2014
summary: For a heteroaryl chloride paired with an unstable heteroaryl boron reagent, ligand, base, and solvent should be optimized as an interacting set.
supporting_excerpt: Catalyst activation, palladium speciation, boron masking or hydrolysis, protodeboronation, phase behavior, and heterocycle coordination can all control the same coupling.
transferability_note: This transfers because the available variables directly represent these interacting controls. The specific optimum remains substrate-dependent and cannot be inferred from one literature condition.
notes: Use factorial or deliberately diverse initial experiments for high-risk heteroaryl pairs.
